analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a flat 20-then-17 percent tax on wages and business profits and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: Senator Shelby's flat tax bill, introduced July 21, 1997 with two Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have scrapped the entire federal income tax system and replaced it with a single flat rate: 20 percent, dropping to 17 percent, on cash wages and business income only. It would repeal the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, all tax credits, and most tax deductions, while taxing nothing from investment income like capital gains, dividends, or interest. It would also cap total federal spending, force reauthorization of 'unearned' benefit programs such as food assistance or face termination, and require a three-fifths vote of both chambers for any future tax increase or spending above the caps.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners would see their top rates fall from 39.6 percent to 20 and then 17 percent, and pay nothing on investment income, since the bill taxes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation. Large estates would stop paying estate and gift taxes entirely. Business owners would pay a 17-20 percent rate on active business income with wages deductible, and would be allowed to withdraw excess assets from company pension plans. Executives would benefit from the repeal of pension compensation caps and nondiscrimination rules. Families would get a larger standard deduction ($22,000 for couples, $5,000 per child) and a far simpler return.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and business owners

how_it_helps.text: Every household gets a large standard deduction ($22,000 joint, $14,400 head of household, $11,000 single, plus $5,000 per dependent), and filing becomes a one-page calculation on wages alone.
The top income tax rate drops from 39.6 percent to 20 percent, and to 17 percent after 1998, and capital gains, dividends, interest, and other investment income fall outside taxable income entirely.
The estate and gift tax is repealed for estates of people dying after 1996, and the alternative minimum tax and all tax credits are repealed.
Businesses pay the flat rate on active business income with wages and inputs deductible, and the corporate income tax, AMT, and most business tax provisions are repealed.
Companies may reclaim excess pension assets without plan termination, and pension nondiscrimination, top-heavy, compensation-limit, and early-distribution-penalty rules are repealed.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary filers would lose every tax credit and deduction except the standard deduction, including mortgage interest, charitable giving, and state tax deductions. Workers with untaxed benefits would effectively be taxed more: government and tax-exempt employers would owe a new 20 percent tax on the value of employee benefits such as health insurance, which would likely come out of wages or benefits. Federal spending would be capped, with shortfalls cut 20 percent from defense and 80 percent from non-defense programs, and every 'unearned entitlement' and most discretionary programs would lose their spending authority unless Congress reauthorized them. Future tax increases or spending above the caps would need a three-fifths vote of each chamber, making it hard to reverse.
analysis.who_pays_short: Benefit recipients, homeowners, and federal programs

drawbacks.text: Only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation are taxed; capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritance income are untaxed, shifting the tax burden toward people who work for a living and away from people who live off investments.
All tax credits and itemized deductions are repealed, so homeowners, charitable donors, and families who currently deduct mortgage interest or state taxes could pay more despite the lower rate.

Spending authority for every 'unearned entitlement' (anything not Social Security, Medicare, veterans' benefits, or earned retirement) and most discretionary programs ends in 1997-1998 unless separately reauthorized, and sequestration would cut 80 percent of any overrun from non-defense accounts.
Government and tax-exempt employers owe a new 20 percent tax on noncash employee benefits like health insurance, raising the cost of public-sector and nonprofit employment.

Companies may take back excess assets from defined-benefit pension plans, and the tax on early and excess retirement distributions is repealed, weakening protections for rank-and-file pension savers while executive contribution limits disappear.

A three-fifths vote of each chamber would be required to raise any income tax rate, cut the standard deduction, create a new tax expenditure, or spend above the caps, locking in the initial tax and spending choices against future majorities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplicity and the big standard deduction would have genuinely helped many working families, and a flatter code is easier to understand. But the design delivers its largest gains to the top of the income scale and to estates, untaxes investment income entirely, strips out deductions and credits that middle-income homeowners and charities rely on, and then locks the whole arrangement in with a three-fifths-vote rule while forcing benefit programs to survive a reauthorization fight. The bill would also have had to be paid for, and the spending caps and entitlement terminations were the offset, with cuts concentrated in non-defense discretionary programs. Honest supporters would have to concede the burden of the trade-off fell unevenly on those least able to bear it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on July 21, 1997, and the committee never acted on it; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Shelby introduced the Freedom and Fairness Restoration Act of 1997 on July 21, 1997, alongside introductory remarks.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced.
Two Republican senators cosponsored the bill.
No further action was ever recorded: the Finance Committee never reported the bill, and it received no vote in the Senate before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing progressive tax structure, the estate tax, itemized deductions, and federal benefit programs all remained intact; high earners and large estates did not receive the tax cuts the bill would have given them, and beneficiaries of means-tested programs were not subjected to a reauthorization-or-termination deadline.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax code and federal programs

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alabama; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Sen. Jesse Helms
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Carolina; cosponsor

against.name: William Roth
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the Finance Committee, never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; it sat without action from referral in July 1997 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three senators behind the bill were Republicans, no Democrats cosponsored it, and the record contains no votes on the bill at any stage.

industries.note: The flat rate, repeal of the AMT, untaxed investment income, and full estate tax repeal deliver the largest dollar savings to top earners and heirs. The revenue those provisions forego would be offset by spending caps and program terminations borne by ordinary households.

Active business income would be taxed at 20 then 17 percent with wages and inputs deductible, and corporate tax provisions and the AMT disappear. Whether workers share the gain would depend on market competition, while the bill's spending caps would cut the government purchasing and programs some businesses serve.

industries.industry: State and local governments and tax-exempt employers
industries.note: They would owe a new 20 percent tax on the value of noncash employee benefits such as health insurance, raising the cost of teachers, nurses, and government workers. That cost would fall on public budgets, nonprofit finances, or employees' own compensation.

industries.industry: Private pension plans and their participants
industries.note: Nondiscrimination, coverage, and executive compensation limits are repealed and companies may claw back excess pension assets, favoring employers and top-paid executives. Early-distribution penalties and required minimum distributions also vanish, which helps some savers but weakens plan protections for rank-and-file workers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A one-page tax on wages minus a standard deduction would sharply reduce demand for professional filing help and complexity-driven products. Ordinary filers who pay for that help would benefit alongside.
